source_document.body:
The National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) Industry Conference convenes researchers, technology providers and industry leaders who use advanced cyberinfrastructure (CI) to accelerate the process of discovery. All wrestle with the same challenges; how to apply the latest innovation for meaningful results without breaking the bank. NCSA was celebrating its 40th anniversary at the October 13-14 event.
Following opening remarks from NCSA Industry Program Director Brendan McGinty, a keynote by Addison Snell, co-founder and chief executive officer of Intersect360 Research , covered a range of topics that inform I-360’s market projections and outlook for the 2030s:
Intersect360 Research CEO Addison Snell (Image courtesy Meg Severson, NCSA)
Power generation, consumption and efficiency;
Geopolitical stability and its influence on national sovereignty;
Technical requirements of consumer-grade artificial intelligence (AI);
Long-term adoption of lower-precision processing for high-performance computing (HPC) applications;
The evolution and adoption of quantum computing;
Data sovereignty for enterprise AI;
Does hyperscale win? What happens to on-prem computing?
Snell’s keynote set the stage for the balance of the agenda that appealed to participants who work with scientific computing, AI infrastructure, healthcare software, digital agriculture, manufacturing, cybersecurity, and technical workforce development. Rather than treating each as independent domains, all were presented within the shared innovation ecosystem that NCSA has served for four decades.
Technology Roadmap
Jack Wells ( Nvidia ), David Griggs ( Dell Technologies ), and Rob Stevenson ( AHEAD ) participated on a panel moderated by J.D. Maloney of NCSA’s Innovative Solutions Lab. This session’s composition highlighted an important feature of contemporary AI infrastructure: Effective computing environments depend on more than accelerator performance. They require agile coordination across compute, memory, networking, storage, software, deployment architecture, and operational support.
“Infrastructure planning must account for the complete workload lifecycle,” said Maloney. “Training a large model, conducting distributed scientific simulations, running inference services, and processing instrument-generated data can impose very different requirements; memory capacity and bandwidth may constrain one application, while communication overhead or storage throughput limit others,” he added. Consequently, selecting a platform requires a holistic understanding of workload behavior rather than an exclusive reliance on peak floating-point performance or advertised accelerator specifications. Software compatibility, scalability, utilization, reliability, and the cost of moving data through the system all impact practical throughput.
The presence of hardware vendors alongside academic and research-computing leaders created the perfect setting in which to analyze these interdependencies. For industry, the central architectural question is not simply which processor is fastest, but which combination of hardware and software delivers useful, reproducible results at an acceptable operational cost.
Surrogate Modeling
A surrogate modeling session with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC) Associate Professor, Civil and Environmental Engineering Hadi Meidani (PhD), and NCSA Research Scientist Qibang Liu (PhD), was moderated by NCSA Industry Senior Program Manager Jeff Terstriep. The panel explored how to reduce simulation cost while retaining the necessary predictive accuracy.
Chris Pond, lead of NCSA’s Research Data Engineering group (Image courtesy Meg Severson, NCSA)
High-fidelity numerical simulations are essential for modeling complex physical systems, from structural behavior and material deformation to fluid dynamics and environmental processes. However, repeatedly running them for design optimization, sensitivity analysis, uncertainty quantification, or probabilistic risk assessment is computationally-costly. Surrogate modeling offers an efficient approximation.
Meidani’s engineering perspective and Liu’s research role at NCSA brought together domain-specific simulation expertise and the computational capabilities needed to develop and evaluate data-driven approaches. For organizations working with computationally expensive models, surrogate modeling offers a pathway toward faster design exploration and more extensive uncertainty analysis—provided that computational savings are balanced with rigorous validation and a clear understanding of model limitations.
Collaborative Software Development for Patient Care
This healthcare-focused session featured MarginDX, represented by NCSA’s Sarah Chronister, Chris Pond and Kenton McHenry (PhD), with Project Agora, presented by Brighten Godfrey (PhD) of UIUC’s Siebel School of Computing and Data Science and the IMMERSE Center for Immersive Computing .
NCSA Deputy Director John Towns (Image courtesy Meg Severson, NCSA)
Healthcare applications often require the integration of heterogeneous data, operational systems, analytical tools and user interfaces. Delivering useful software in a compliant environment involves data interoperability, access control, reproducibility, and maintainability, while adhering to clinical workflow requirements. Data engineering is important; analytical pipelines must preserve provenance, handle inconsistent inputs and make transformations auditable. Where patient information is involved, privacy controls and appropriate authorization must be integrated into the system architecture rather than added as an afterthought.
Scientific AI: From Models to Research Workflows
This session, moderated by NCSA’s Katherine Kendig, featured Eliu Huerta (PhD), lead for translational AI at Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago , and Andrew Smith (PhD), professor of bioengineering at UIUC; also affiliated with the UIUC Cancer Center. With participation by researchers from a national laboratory and a university research center, this panel reflected the interdisciplinary character of scientific AI. Its placement after the infrastructure discussion helped participants understand bioengineering’s translational benefits to many other domains.
Quantum Computing
Elizabeth Goldschmidt (PhD), associate professor of physics, and director of the Illinois Quantum Information Science and Technology Center (IQUIST), presented the session on quantum computing at UIUC. Goldschmidt explained that quantum computing introduces a fundamentally different computational paradigm. Potential applications include selected problems in chemistry, materials science, cryptography, and other areas which are difficult to efficiently simulate via classical methods.
She further emphasized that quantum computing is unlikely to replace conventional HPC any time soon (or ever). Current quantum platforms face substantial constraints involving noise, error correction, circuit depth, hardware connectivity, and the overhead of preparing and measuring quantum states. Practical progress depends on matching specific algorithms to hardware capabilities and identifying problems for which quantum approaches could offer a meaningful advantage. Classical simulation, optimization and data-processing infrastructure will remain important components of many quantum workflows.
UIUC’s quantum research ecosystem provides an institutional setting for connecting fundamental research with technology development. For industry participants, the relevant questions include which application classes merit early investigation, how quantum workloads might integrate with existing computational pipelines and the expertise organizations must develop before the technology matures.
Women in AI and the Human Infrastructure of Innovation
Sharon Donovan (PhD) of NCSA’s Personalized Nutrition Initiative, Stephanie Potisek Lee (PhD) of Dow and Jessica Wedow (PhD) of AIFarms served on a Women in AI panel moderated by NCSA’s Misha Shah. Their range of perspectives, including research, industry and agriculture, highlighted a variety of organizational environments in which AI systems are developed and deployed.
(Image courtesy Meg Severson, NCSA)
Technical innovation depends on the availability of expertise across disciplines, and the structures that enable people to effectively contribute. All must develop pathways for technical leadership, support collaboration across specialties and ensure that teams can evaluate problems from multiple perspectives. For AI engineering, diversity of experience can be particularly valuable when defining requirements, selecting evaluation criteria and identifying failure modes that a homogeneous team might overlook. The future AI and quantum workforce must leave no stone unturned. Related career-paths, and identifiable role models, must be presented to all youths so that more can begin to envision themselves making this journey.
NCSA: From Advanced Computing to Co-Development
The second day opened with a keynote by NCSA Deputy Director John Towns titled, “NCSA: From Advanced Computing to Co-Development.” After describing the many facets of NCSA service and support, he asked the audience to bring one consequential research and development challenge to their team that could be explored, prototyped or scaled together.
Towns’ speech was followed by a workforce panel moderated by UIUC Associate Chancellor for Strategic Partnerships and Initiatives Kim Kidwell (PhD). Panelists included Jack Wells (PhD) of Nvidia, Erik Hagberg (PhD) of Archer Daniels Midland (ADM), and Masha Trenhaile of Bayer Crop Sciences .
While these organizations operate in different sectors (with varied regulatory and business frameworks), all face the same challenge of translating emerging innovation into useful applications. All need hybrid talent – professionals who understand distributed systems, data engineering, scientific computing, AI evaluation, infrastructure operations, cybersecurity, and the relevant software stack.
Anita Nikolich of the UIUC School of Information Sciences (Image courtesy Meg Severson, NCSA)
Education and workforce development must therefore connect theoretical foundations with practical experience. Working with realistic datasets, distributed computing environments, reproducible pipelines, and production-oriented constraints helps prepare practitioners for the complexity of real deployments. The panel’s mix of computing, agriculture, and industrial research leadership provided a cross-sector framework for considering such challenges.
NCSA Centers and Research Infrastructure
The NCSA Center Spotlight, moderated by Bill Kramer (PhD) of the New Frontiers Initiative , featured Vlad Kindratenko (DSc), director of the NCSA Center for AI Innovation, Ansh Ankul, lead AI research engineer at the Center for Digital Agriculture and Brett Bode (PhD) of the Delta Project Office.
Their perspectives represented complementary elements of an advanced-computing ecosystem: AI research and engineering, domain-specific applications and research infrastructure. The combination matters because computational research is rarely confined to a single layer of the technology stack. A project may require specialized hardware, data preparation, distributed execution, model development, and application-specific validation.
Shared research-computing environments can also reduce the barrier to experimentation by delivering access to capabilities that would be too expensive or impractical for individual teams to maintain. Their challenge is to provide that access while maintaining performance, reliability, security, and effective resource utilization.
Phuong Cao (PhD), cybersecurity research specialist at NCSA (Image courtesy Meg Severson, NCSA)
For industrial collaborators, engagement with a research center, like NCSA, provides a pathway to specialized expertise and computational resources, and the ability to road-test new strategies before committing them to large-scale deployment.
Trust But Verify: AI Security and Assurance
The final technical session addressed cybersecurity challenges associated with AI and quantum technologies, and was led by Anita Nikolich of the UIUC School of Information Sciences and Phuong Cao (PhD), cybersecurity research specialist at NCSA and National Science Foundation (NSF) Trusted CI Fellow.
Nikolich explained that organizations must consider attacks on model inputs, data poisoning, information leakage, compromised dependencies, and the misuse of AI-enabled tools. Systems that incorporate external data or invoke tools autonomously can create additional pathways through which untrusted inputs influence behavior. “Trust in an AI result depends on the GPUs, schedulers and cryptography beneath them,” said Cao.
Sunrise over the South Farms; I-Hotel room with a view. (Photo by the author)
Quantum computing, and the dreaded “Q-Day,” raise a different concern: sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computers will undermine widely deployed public-key cryptographic systems based on integer factorization or discrete logarithms. This does not mean that today’s quantum computers can routinely break modern encryption, but its arrival establishes quantum cryptographic transition planning as a priority. While most predict that quantum systems will take more time to perfect, Nikolich shared that Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora recently warned that hostile nation-states could possess cryptanalytically-relevant quantum computers by 2029 (or sooner). The technology could break current public-key cryptography and will therefore command major revisions of global security infrastructure in the coming years.
To prepare, Nikolich urges organizations to inventory cryptographic dependencies, assess exposure to long-lived sensitive data and develop migration strategies toward standardized post-quantum cryptography where appropriate. These efforts can be complex because cryptography is embedded in protocols, devices, software libraries, and third-party services.
Cao leads NSF projects on a security data lake built from experience with national CI, and therefore brings real-world metrics to the migration question. His team’s Post-Quantum Cryptography Network Instrument (IEEE QCE 2024) measures how widely post-quantum cryptography has been adopted and can identify safe migration pathways. Another of his IEEE QCE 2024 studies measured network alerts in a security operations center and sorted them into three categories: true attacks, attack attempts and benign events. Finally, a more recent study measured how larger post-quantum certificate chains delay the “time to first byte” in transport layer security (TLS) connections. These studies helped to inform a project Cao leads on quantum-resistant cryptography for supercomputing applications where new algorithms are tested with scientific codes running on NCSA systems.
Conclusion: Integration Is the Central Engineering Challenge
The NCSA Industry Conference presented a broad view of advanced computing. For industry leadership, the conference established practical priorities: benchmark infrastructure against real workloads; use surrogate models where they can accelerate validated simulation workflows; treat data quality and reproducibility as foundational engineering concerns; evaluate AI in the context of scientific objectives; aggressively plan for evolving security requirements; and invest in hybrid talent that combines computing expertise with data science and domain knowledge.
About the author: Elizabeth Leake is an HPCwire contributor and founder of STEM-Trek, a global nonprofit that supports underrepresented STEM scholars with travel and professional development. She is also a p roject manager of advanced cyberinfrastructure at Texas A&M University.
